prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation as clocks with uncertainty near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I moved B002 to the top of my list after reading the openings. It meets the test I apply most strictly: an original, experimentally verified result that opened a door. Katori's magic-wavelength idea let many atoms be held in a lattice without shifting the clock transition, and the first strontium lattice clock followed. Independent laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg) now agree at the 10^-18 level, and the redefinition of the second is under discussion. It also feeds tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. Seven of eight members ranked it, two of them first, which is much broader support than any other shortlisted topic. That is not merit in itself, but several colleagues who know atomic physics better than I do judge it mature and distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize, and I find their reasoning on the science sound.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is my own criterion that the prize goes to the original experiment and not to the second group that did it much better. Katori proposed the lattice and made the first demonstration. Ye's group then took the accuracy and stability to the extreme, and that is a later, more spectacular realisation. I would want the record on priority between the two reviewed before I accept the pair without qualification. A second concern is that this lineage already has prizes (Hall and Haensch 2005, Wineland 2012). The motivation must name what is new: the magic-wavelength lattice and its metrological consequences, not clocks or combs in general. I also note that Lemonde, Takamoto and the ion-clock community are not credited.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first. She argues that Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the trapping-light shift, that Ye's group delivered the extreme accuracy and the redshift measurements, and that the field is mature, with the redefinition of the second under discussion. She also admits she has not checked priority of the magic-wavelength proposal, since parallel groups discussed it.
responses.response: I agree on the science and have shifted toward her view. Her own caveat is the real issue. If the magic-wavelength proposal has parallel claimants, my standard of finding the people who did the original work means we need that chronology confirmed, ideally through the first lattice-clock demonstrations. I do not think that undoes the pair. The experimental record points to Katori's first Sr lattice clock, with Ye's group an independent, rapid and decisive second demonstration. But we should settle the point before we write a citation that says who proposed what.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ class first and puts twisted bilayer graphene third. He praises the Bistritzer-MacDonald mechanism, but says the superconducting pairing is unsettled, credit for earlier twistronics ideas and the junior experimental lead is complicated, and the recognition may come slightly early. He ranks optical lattice clocks only eighth, because of overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: His maturity point on B038 is fair and it has weakened my first-place ranking for it. The phenomena are well replicated, but the field is moving fast and he is right that Cao's role makes the experimental credit awkward. I do not accept the clock-overlap objection as I understand it. Combs measure optical frequency and the 2012 prize used single trapped ions. The lattice clock rests on a different idea, trapping many atoms without perturbing the transition, and it is verified. I agree the motivation must state that difference precisely. I would not call the KPZ case weak, but I cannot tell from my own work whether the experimental confirmation by Takeuchi is the original result the statutes require.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and the Higgs second. He ranks the clock fourth, but says it is outside his expertise and asks whether the committee sees a clock as a discovery or as technology. For IceCube he argues that the diffuse flux is robust and confirmed in several channels even though most sources are unidentified.
responses.response: His discovery-versus-technology question is the right one, and I answer it as follows. The prize can go to an invention, and a new tool that makes previously unseeable phenomena measurable qualifies when its use is demonstrated. The clocks have been used for redshift tests and clock comparisons, so this is more than an instrument demonstration. On IceCube I accept his case that the diffuse flux is established, and that is why I keep B043 as an alternative. But with the source identification still thin I would hold it a few years, and the credit among Halzen, Spiering and the DUMAND and Baikal pioneers has to be settled first.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs experimental discovery first. He says the 2013 prize recognised only the mechanism, that ATLAS and CMS confirm one another, and that Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are a defensible three-person set as proposers and long-standing leaders.
responses.response: I agree that the discovery is verified and historic. I disagree that the credited names answer our statutory problem. Spokespersons and project leaders directed the instrument. I cannot show from this file that they did the decisive measurement, and a prize for the discovery would then name people for directing the instrument and not for the original experiment. That is why I ranked B053 only sixth. I would need a convincing argument that three named individuals stand for the collaborations, and I do not think we have one. He concedes that his own attribution rests on background knowledge he has not verified, and so does mine.

uncertainties: Chronology and priority of the magic-wavelength lattice proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations (Katori versus Ye, Lemonde and others) needs to be confirmed against the record.
Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes leave enough distinct content for a clock prize, and how the citation should word that difference.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene (B038) is ripe enough that I should still prefer it, given the unsettled pairing mechanism and the question of crediting Cao.
I read only part of the opening ballots in this simulation (those of Danielsson on B053, Lindroth, Mehlig, Pearce and my own), so I have not weighed the arguments of Eriksson, Johansson and Kroll.
statement.conflict_note: I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo (since 2025) and have had long-running exchanges with its community, and Katori is at the University of Tokyo, so there is a possible institutional connection to my preferred configuration that the committee should weigh. I know of no personal collaboration with Katori or Ye in my profile. I also have ties to the Tohoku microscopy community, which is relevant to B025 (Miyazaki), and my Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson is on the committee, but no shortlisted candidate is from Chalmers.
